learningObjectives.text: Explain that Greek heroic excellence is shaped by the source and story-world, not by one universal definition.
Distinguish Achilles’ martial anger and honor-centered story from Odysseus’ cunning, travel, and endurance.

narrativeBlocks.title: Hero is not a moral certificate
narrativeBlocks.body: A Greek hero can be admirable, terrifying, clever, destructive, or all four at once. The word marks a certain status and story-world; it does not automatically mean “good person.”

narrativeBlocks.title: Two openings, two heroic pressures
narrativeBlocks.body: Achilles asks what honor costs when anger takes over. Odysseus asks whether intelligence and endurance can bring a person home. Both are heroic; neither is a universal template.

narrativeBlocks.title: Keep the source attached
narrativeBlocks.body: Later writers and adaptations often blend heroic traits into one tidy canon. Project Mythos keeps the source attached, so you can see which version says what.

quiz.prompt: What does the Iliad’s opening foreground?
quiz.explanation: Achilles’ anger and its cost. Revisit the named passage and distinguish its narrative from the lesson’s interpretation.

quiz.prompt: How does the Odyssey’s opening differ?

choices.text: It begins with the Nemean lion.
It foregrounds a widely travelled hero and his return.
It begins with Achilles’ refusal of gifts.
